🧠 Brain Blood Supply

Lecture created by Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen · Batch 44 CNS Series

Progress 0/13

🧠 Course Roadmap & Objectives

  • Understand the internal carotid and vertebral arterial systems.
  • Understand the circle of Willis.
  • Understand the venous drainage of the brain.
Key concept: The brain's arterial supply consists of two paired vessel systems: the two internal carotid arteries (right & left) and the two vertebral arteries (right & left). The two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery at the medulla–pons junction. Hence the two divisions used throughout neuroanatomy: Anterior circulation = two ICAs + branches, and Posterior circulation = two vertebral arteries + branches.
Normal cerebral blood flow ≈ 50 mL/100 g brain tissue/min. The brain receives about 15% of cardiac output yet consumes 20% of total body oxygen.

🩸 Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) — Course ⭐⭐ High Yield

  • Enters the cranium via the carotid canal of the temporal bone.
  • Lies within the cavernous sinus as the carotid siphon (S-shaped course).
  • Supplies tributaries to the dura mater, hypophysis, tympanic cavity, and trigeminal ganglion.
  • Gives branches to the optic nerve, optic chiasm, hypothalamus, and genu of the internal capsule.
Endovascular (7-segment) classification (C1–C7): Interventional radiologists / neurosurgeons performing catheter-based (endovascular) procedures divide the ICA anatomically into 7 segments, C1 through C7 (C = Carotid). Order of major branches from proximal to distal: Ophthalmic → Posterior communicating → Anterior choroidal → terminal bifurcation (ACA + MCA).

🌿 ICA Branches — Memorize the Order

Order to memorize: 1. Ophthalmic → 2. Posterior communicating (PComA) → 3. Anterior choroidal (AChA) → 4. Anterior cerebral (ACA) → 5. Anterior communicating (AComA) → 6. Middle cerebral (MCA)
1️⃣ Ophthalmic Artery
  • Enters the apex of the orbit via the optic canal together with the optic nerve (CN II).
  • Central artery of the retina: a branch of the ophthalmic artery that runs with the optic nerve; it provides the only blood supply to the inner aspect of the retina.
  • It is an end artery — occlusion results directly in blindness.
⭐⭐⭐ Exam pearl: "end artery + only supply" → occlusion = irreversible monocular blindness (central retinal artery occlusion).
2️⃣ Posterior Communicating Artery (PComA)
  • Joins the posterior cerebral artery and the internal carotid artery — the anastomotic link between anterior & posterior circulations.
  • Supplies the optic chiasm, optic tract, hypothalamus, subthalamus, and the anterior half of the ventral-inferior thalamus.
  • A common site of berry (saccular) aneurysm.
🚨 Clinical: PComA aneurysm compresses CN III (oculomotor) → oculomotor palsy: ptosis, "down-and-out" eye (squint), and diplopia, ± pupil dilation.
3️⃣ Anterior Choroidal Artery (AChA)
  • Supplies the choroid plexus of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle.
  • Supplies hippocampus, amygdala, lateral geniculate body, globus pallidus, and part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
  • Supplies the proximal part of the optic radiation as fibers leave the lateral geniculate body to form Meyer's loop.
Optic pathway order: Optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate body → optic radiation (Meyer's loop) → visual cortex.
4️⃣ Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA)
  • One of the two terminal branches of the ICA (with MCA).
  • Supplies the medial surface of the frontal & parietal lobes and the corpus callosum.
  • Supplies part of the corpus striatum and anterior limb of internal capsule via the medial striate artery (of Heubner).
  • Supplies the leg and foot area of the motor/sensory cortex (paracentral lobule) — medial homunculus = lower limb.
  • Segments: A1 = pre-communicating (ICA bifurcation → AComA); A2 = post-communicating (after AComA).
  • Two key cortical branches: callosomarginal (runs anterior to corpus callosum) and pericallosal (runs in the corpus callosum itself).
🚨 ACA occlusion → contralateral lower-limb paralysis (leg/foot > arm/face), since ACA supplies the medial (leg) homunculus.
5️⃣ Anterior Communicating Artery (AComA)
  • Connects the two anterior cerebral arteries.
  • The commonest site of berry aneurysm in the brain.
6️⃣ Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)
  • The other terminal branch of the ICA — supplies the lateral convexity of the hemisphere and the insula.
  • Supplies trunk, arm, and face areas of the motor/sensory cortex, and Broca's & Wernicke's speech areas.
  • Supplies the striatum, pallidum, and anterior/posterior limbs of the internal capsule via the lateral striate arteries.
  • Divided into a superficial part (superior + inferior, split by the lateral sulcus / Sylvian fissure) and a deep part.
  • Endovascular segments: M1–M4.
🧠 "Opercula" = the cortex overlying/lining the Sylvian (lateral) fissure — imagine the fissure as a mouth: frontoparietal opercula = upper lip, temporal operculum = lower lip. Hence fronto-opercular, parieto-opercular, temporo-opercular arteries. Any artery named "opercular" → think Sylvian fissure region.
🚨 MCA occlusion (most common stroke site) → contralateral arm & face weakness > leg, aphasia (if dominant hemisphere), homonymous hemianopia, gaze deviation toward the lesion.
⭐⭐⭐ Exam trap: The middle cerebral artery is NOT part of the circle of Willis — only its ICA "parent" segment feeds into the circle.

🧵 Vertebrobasilar (Posterior Circulation) System

Posterior circulation = the two vertebral arteries and their branches. The two vertebral arteries unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the single basilar artery (BA).

A. Vertebral Artery (VA) Branches

Anterior Spinal Artery (ASA)

One branch arises from the right VA and one from the left VA; the two unite in the midline to form a single anterior spinal artery running along the anterior median fissure of the spinal cord.

Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA)
  • Gives rise to the posterior spinal artery.
  • Supplies the dorsolateral medulla.
  • Supplies the inferior surface of the cerebellum and the choroid plexus of the 4th ventricle.
  • Supplies the medial & inferior vestibular nuclei, inferior cerebellar peduncle, nucleus ambiguus, intra-axial fibers of CN IX & CN X, spinothalamic tract, and spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract.
  • Supplies the hypothalamospinal tract to the ciliospinal center (of Budge) at T1–T2 → involved in Horner syndrome.
⭐⭐⭐ PICA occlusion = Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome — the classic "PICA picks a peck of cranial nerves" territory.

B. Basilar Artery (BA) — "Formed by the joining of the two vertebral arteries"

1. Pontine Arteries (PA)

Penetrating and short circumferential branches. Supply corticospinal tracts and the intra-axial fibers of the abducent nerve (CN VI).

2. Labyrinthine Artery (LA)

Supplies the inner ear. Runs alongside CN VII & CN VIII toward the internal acoustic meatus.

3. Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA)
  • Supplies the inferior surface of the cerebellum.
  • Supplies the facial motor nucleus and intra-axial fibers of CN VII, vestibular nuclei, cochlear nuclei, intra-axial fibers of CN VIII, spinothalamic tract, and inferior/middle cerebellar peduncles.
  • Gives rise to the labyrinthine artery in 85% of people.
  • Supplies the hypothalamospinal tract (Horner syndrome).
4. Superior Cerebellar Artery (SCA)

Supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum and the cerebellar nuclei; supplies the rostral & lateral pons including the superior cerebellar peduncle and spinothalamic tract.

🚨 SCA aneurysm can compress CN V (trigeminal) → trigeminal neuralgia ("the worst pain ever"). Treatment may include microvascular decompression surgery to separate the artery from the nerve.
5. Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)
  • Forms the terminal branches of the basilar artery.
  • Provides the major blood supply to the midbrain.
  • Supplies the posterior half of the thalamus and the medial & lateral geniculate bodies.
  • Supplies the occipital lobe, visual cortex, and inferior surface of the temporal lobe (including the hippocampal formation).
  • Gives rise to the lateral & medial posterior choroidal arteries, which supply the thalamus, pineal body, and choroid plexus of the 3rd & lateral ventricles.
🚨 PCA occlusion → contralateral homonymous hemianopia (with macular sparing), visual agnosia, thalamic pain syndrome, midbrain (CN III) signs.

⭕ Circle of Willis — Interactive Numbered Atlas

Formed by: 1) Anterior communicating · 2) Anterior cerebral · 3) Internal carotid · 4) Posterior communicating · 5) Posterior cerebral arteries. Gives off penetrating arteries to the inferior aspect supplying the hypothalamus, subthalamus, thalamus, and midbrain. The MCA is NOT part of the circle.

📷 Angiography Correlation

🛡️ Meningeal Arteries (ECA branches)

Three meningeal arteries, all branches of the external carotid artery (ECA): 1. Anterior · 2. Middle · 3. Posterior meningeal arteries.

1. Anterior Meningeal Arteries

Arise from the anterior & posterior ethmoidal arteries. Supply the dura mater of the anterior cranial fossa.

2. Middle Meningeal Artery ⭐⭐⭐
  • A branch of the maxillary artery.
  • Enters the cranium via the foramen spinosum.
  • Lies between the periosteal and meningeal layers of dura, deep into the temporal & parietal bones.
  • Supplies most of the dura mater.
🚨 Laceration → epidural hemorrhage (extradural hematoma): biconvex (lens-shaped) lesion on CT, classic lucid interval (seen in ~50% of cases); skull fractures typically found. Classic trauma: temporal bone fracture / blow to the pterion, often from a hammer/blunt object as illustrated.
3. Posterior Meningeal Arteries

Branches of the ascending pharyngeal, vertebral, and occipital arteries. Supply the dura mater of the posterior cranial fossa.

🔵 Veins of the Brain

Cerebral veins are devoid of valves and lie along the surface sulci; they drain from the cortex & subcortical substance and terminate in the dural sinuses.

A. Superficial Cerebral Veins

  • Drain into the superior sagittal sinus as bridging veins.
  • Laceration of these vessels results in subdural hemorrhage (hematoma).
  • Mainly 3 veins: superior, middle, and inferior.

B. Deep Cerebral Veins

Drain the deep subcortical structures of the cerebral hemispheres: septal area, thalamus, and basal nuclei.

1. Internal cerebral veins drain: (a) septal vein, (b) thalamostriate vein, (c) terminal vein, (d) venous angle — the point where the septal & thalamostriate veins meet, marking the location of the interventricular foramen of Monro.

2. Great cerebral vein (of Galen): receives blood from the internal cerebral veins and drains into the straight sinus.

🚨 Bridging vein tear (often after minor trauma, especially elderly/atrophic brains) → subdural hematoma: crescent-shaped on CT, crosses suture lines, may present with a delayed/insidious course — contrast with the biconvex, suture-limited epidural hematoma.

🕳️ Venous Dural Sinuses ⭐⭐ High Yield

  • Endothelium-lined valveless channels whose walls are formed by the periosteal and meningeal layers of dura mater.
  • Collect blood from the superficial & deep cerebral veins, diploic veins, and emissary veins.
  • Receive arachnoid granulations and absorb cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
🧠 10 named dural sinuses (order to memorize): Superior sagittal → Inferior sagittal → Straight → Left & right transverse → Confluence of the sinuses → Sigmoid → Sphenoparietal → Superior petrosal → Inferior petrosal → Cavernous.
1. Superior Sagittal Sinus (SSS)

Runs in the midline superiorly, from the anterior skull to the posterior skull. Extends from the foramen cecum to the internal occipital protuberance, usually terminating in the right transverse sinus. Receives blood from superficial cerebral veins, diploic veins, and emissary veins. Receives most arachnoid granulations.

2. Inferior Sagittal Sinus

Courses in the inferior (free) edge of the falx cerebri. Joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus.

3. Straight Sinus

Formed by the junction of the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the inferior sagittal sinus. Runs along the line where the falx cerebri meets the tentorium cerebelli (the dural partition between the brain and cerebellum). Terminates at the internal occipital protuberance and usually drains into the left transverse sinus. Drains the superior surface of the cerebellum.

4. Confluence of the Sinuses

Lies at the internal occipital protuberance (deep to the external/posterior occipital protuberance you can palpate). Formed by the union of the superior sagittal, straight, and transverse sinuses.

5. Left & Right Transverse Sinuses

Originate at the confluence of the sinuses and course anterolaterally along the edge of the tentorium cerebelli (deep to the superior nuchal line, running roughly toward the mastoid/ear) to become the sigmoid sinus at the point where the superior petrosal sinuses join.

6. Sigmoid Sinus

A continuation of the transverse sinus at the superior petrosal sinus. Passes inferiorly and medially into the jugular foramen to become the internal jugular vein.

7. Sphenoparietal Sinus

Lies along the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone and drains into the cavernous sinus.

8. Superior Petrosal Sinus

Extends from the cavernous sinus to the junction of the transverse and sigmoid sinuses. Receives tributaries from the pons, medulla, cerebellum, and inner ear.

9. Inferior Petrosal Sinus

Passes between CN IX (glossopharyngeal) and CN X (vagus) and drains into the internal jugular vein after exiting the skull via the jugular foramen. Drains the inferior cerebellum, cavernous sinus, and clival plexus.

10. Cavernous Sinus ⭐⭐⭐
  • Surrounds the sella turcica and body of the sphenoid bone.
  • Contains, within the sinus: the internal carotid artery, its periarterial (sympathetic) plexus, and CN VI (abducent).
  • Contains, in the lateral wall: CN III (oculomotor), CN IV (trochlear), and the ophthalmic (V1) & maxillary (V2) branches of CN V (trigeminal).
  • Receives blood from the superior & inferior ophthalmic veins of the orbit.
🧠 Mnemonic for cavernous sinus contents — "O TOM CAT": Ophthalmic vein / Trochlear (IV) / Oculomotor (III) / Maxillary (V2) — lateral wall; Carotid (ICA) / Abducent (VI) / Trigeminal ophthalmic (V1) — within the sinus.

PComA aneurysmCompresses CN III → ptosis, "down-and-out" eye, diplopia ± dilated pupil
SCA aneurysmCompresses CN V → trigeminal neuralgia
ACA occlusionContralateral lower-limb paralysis > upper limb
MCA occlusionContralateral face & arm weakness > leg, aphasia (dominant), hemianopia
PCA occlusionContralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
PICA occlusionLateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome

AComAMost common site of berry aneurysm overall
PComAClassic site of berry aneurysm causing CN III palsy

Berry (Saccular) vs. Fusiform Aneurysm

Berry / saccular aneurysm: Focal weakness of the tunica media → the intima balloons outward on one side only — like a hernia of the vessel wall. Sac/berry-shaped. Common at arterial branch points (AComA > PComA > MCA bifurcation).
Fusiform aneurysm: Dilation involves the entire circumference of the vessel — spindle-shaped, symmetric outpouching on both sides.

Homunculus Correlation

The medial hemisphere surface (ACA territory) represents the lower limb. The lateral hemisphere surface (MCA territory) represents the face, arm, and hand — the largest cortical territory, which is why MCA strokes are the most common and most disabling.

🧠 Mnemonics & Memory Aids

ICA branch order: "Old People Always Ask About Medicine" → Ophthalmic, PCom, AChoroidal, ACA, ACom, MCA.
Circle of Willis components: "2 Communicating + 2 Cerebral(ant) + 1 Carotid + 2 Cerebral(post)" = AComA, 2×ACA, 2×ICA, PComA (x2), 2×PCA. MCA is excluded.
Cavernous sinus contents: "O TOM CAT" (see Dural Sinuses section).
Dural sinus drainage pathway: SSS + Straight → Confluence → Transverse → Sigmoid → Internal jugular vein.
Opercular = Sylvian fissure — any artery name containing "opercular" (fronto-, parieto-, temporo-opercular) is traveling in/around the lateral sulcus.
PICA vs AICA vs SCA (cerebellar surfaces): PICA = Posterior-inferior, AICA = Anterior-inferior, SCA = Superior. All three from the vertebrobasilar system, one for each cerebellar surface.
Aneurysm shape: "Berry = one side (like a berry on a stem)"; "Fusiform = spindle-form, both sides."

⚡ Rapid Revision / Exam-Cram Sheet

Anterior Circulation (2× ICA)

  1. Ophthalmic — retina, end artery
  2. PComA — links to PCA; berry aneurysm → CN III palsy
  3. AChA — internal capsule, hippocampus, LGB
  4. ACA (A1/A2) — medial surface, leg homunculus
  5. AComA — most common aneurysm site
  6. MCA (M1–M4) — lateral surface, face/arm, speech areas

Posterior Circulation (2× VA → BA)

  1. VA → PICA, Anterior spinal a.
  2. BA → Pontine aa.
  3. BA → Labyrinthine a. (85% from AICA)
  4. BA → AICA
  5. BA → SCA — CN V, trigeminal neuralgia
  6. BA → PCA (terminal) — midbrain, thalamus, occipital lobe

Circle of Willis = 5 named vessels

AComA — 2×ACA — 2×ICA — 2×PComA — 2×PCA (MCA excluded)

Dural Sinus Chain

SSS ⟶ (+Straight) ⟶ Confluence ⟶ Transverse (R/L) ⟶ Sigmoid ⟶ Internal jugular vein · Cavernous ⟶ Sup./Inf. petrosal ⟶ Transverse/Sigmoid & IJV
